title: How to Find Referral Leads as a Real Estate Referral Agent
metaDesc: Where referral-only real estate agents actually find leads to send: your existing network, past clients, and even your own transactions. A practical guide.
h1: How to Find Referral Leads as a Real Estate Referral Agent
about: Where a real estate referral agent finds people to refer, once they've stepped back from active sales
answer: Referral leads come from the network you already built while actively selling: past clients, family, friends, neighbors, and people from church, school, or trade groups. You can also refer clients on your own transactions and accept referrals from agents in other states who don’t have a Florida connection.
takeaways: Your best referral leads are people who already trust you: past clients, family, friends, and neighbors.
You don't need new marketing to find them; you already know who's likely to move in the next few years.
Past clients often come back for a second home, a downsize, or a referral of their own kids or parents.
You can refer yourself, on your own purchase or sale, and other agents can refer their out-of-area clients to you.
Staying lightly visible (a holiday card, a check-in call, a social post) keeps you top of mind without active marketing.
tldr: A referral agent's leads come from the relationships they already have: past clients, family, friends, and community connections, plus incoming referrals from agents elsewhere who need a trusted Florida contact. No MLS, no marketing budget, no active prospecting required.
body:
Where do referral leads actually come from?

The honest answer: the same people you already know. Referral income doesn’t require new marketing or prospecting. It runs on the relationships you built during your active years, or simply the people already in your life: past clients, family, friends, neighbors, coworkers, and people from church, school, or a trade organization you belong to.

Do past clients really come back?

Often, yes. A past buyer or seller may reach out years later because they’re moving again, downsizing, buying a second home, or helping their own adult child buy a first place. If you stayed on good terms, you’re usually still the person they think of first, even if you’re not actively selling anymore. You just need to be reachable when they do.

Can you refer yourself?

Yes. If you personally buy or sell a property, you can refer that transaction to an active agent (sometimes yourself through the brokerage’s active side, or another agent) and earn a fee on it, the same as any other referral. It’s a detail many new referral agents don’t realize applies to their own deals.

Do referrals ever come to you instead?

Yes, and this can be a real source of income too. Agents in other states sometimes have a client moving to Florida, or a Florida client moving elsewhere, and need a licensed local contact to hand the deal to. Being part of an established local brokerage’s referral network makes you visible to those incoming referrals, not just the ones you send out.

How much active effort does this take?

Very little, by design. Most referral agents stay lightly visible rather than actively marketing: an occasional check-in call, a holiday card, a quiet social media presence. The goal is to remain the person people think of, not to generate new leads from scratch. If you want to actively market for referrals, you can, but it’s not required to earn.

What if you don’t have decades of past clients yet?

You still have a network, even if it’s smaller. Family, friends, coworkers, neighbors, and people from a church, gym, or trade group all count. The math still works in your favor: you only need one referral every so often for the license to pay for itself, not a constant pipeline. Someone who was licensed only briefly before stepping back can still refer effectively; it’s about who trusts you, not how many closings you had.

What should you avoid doing?

Don’t treat an old client list like a cold-call script. Reaching out to people you haven’t spoken to in years with an obvious sales pitch tends to backfire. A genuine check-in, congratulating someone on a life event, or simply being reachable when they think of real estate on their own, works better than pushing for a referral directly. The relationship comes first; the referral follows naturally when the timing is real.

Does the size of the brokerage you refer into matter?

It can. A larger brokerage with more agents and a wider service area gives you more places to send a referral well, whether your contact is buying in Daytona Beach, downsizing in Ormond Beach, or looking somewhere else in Volusia or Flagler County. A referral that lands with the right specialist agent is more likely to actually close, which is what earns you the fee.

How do you actually make the introduction?

Simply: a warm hand-off, not a formal process. A short call, text, or email connecting your contact directly with the active agent, letting them know you trust this person to take care of them, is usually all it takes. From there, the active agent handles showings, offers, and paperwork; your job is done once the connection is made and the referral agreement is signed between the brokerages.

Where does Adams, Cameron & Co. fit in?

Adams, Cameron & Co., the area’s largest brokerage since 1963 with roughly 300 agents across the region, runs a Realty Referral Program built for exactly this: a place to keep your license active while you refer clients from your own network into a large, trusted local team of agents. Start a conversation if you have a network worth putting to work.

faq.q: Do I need to actively market to earn referral income?
faq.a: No. Most referral income comes from your existing network, past clients, family, friends, and community connections, rather than new marketing. Some agents choose to stay lightly visible with a holiday card or occasional check-in, but active prospecting isn't required.

faq.q: Can I refer my own real estate purchase or sale?
faq.a: Yes. If you personally buy or sell property, you can refer that transaction to an active agent and earn a referral fee on it, the same as referring anyone else.

faq.q: Can referrals come to me instead of me sending them out?
faq.a: Yes. Agents in other states or markets sometimes need a licensed local contact for a client moving to or from your area. Being part of an established brokerage's referral network makes you visible to those incoming referrals too.

faq.q: How long after I stop actively selling can I still generate referral leads?
faq.a: Indefinitely, as long as your license stays active with a referral program. Past clients and personal connections don't expire; people you helped years ago may still reach out when they're ready to move again.
